*Preface: This supplementary document was produced with the assistance and auditing of ChatGPT/Codex (5.6 Sol, High). The complexity of protein dose response calculations as relative to body mass (i.e., g/kg/day) given the heterogeneity of reporting across studies, in addition to the calculation and appropriate propagation of sampling error for this, was not considered in sufficient detail during our planning and pre-registration. As such, calculation from reported data within our code pipelines and data structures was not prepared in advance and proceeded in a somewhat ad hoc basis with calculations being done within the extraction spreadsheets. This presents an issue for human checking, hence prior to analysis and with the assistance of a human for all checking, reviewing, and performance of the manual editing, ChatGPT/Codex (5.6 Sol, High) was used to check the extracted data in this regard, including formulas used, and cross reference against the study pdfs flagging all issues for checking. After this it then proceeded to collate the various methods depending on the reported data in order to transparently report the approaches taken to calculation of protein doses and propagation of uncertainty.*

# Purpose and scope

Protein intake was not reported in a common form across the included studies. Total protein exposure was therefore taken directly from a report when possible or reconstructed from reported dietary intake, supplement composition and schedule, energy intake, percentage energy from protein, and body mass. This document records the calculation rules and provides a study-level register of every protein-related cell that retains an auditable formula in the extraction workbook.

Most calculations were performed during extraction rather than in the analysis pipeline. The study register is therefore exhaustive for retained workbook formulas, but it cannot prove the provenance of a hardcoded value when the intermediate calculation was not retained. Hardcoded values matched to an adjacent formula pattern or to a source table are identified in the audit notes rather than presented as independently reproducible calculations.

# Core assumptions

1. Inputs were converted to compatible units before combination.
2. Directly reported total protein intake in g/kg/day was preferred to a reconstruction when available.
3. A prescribed fixed dose contributed no additional variance on the scale on which it was fixed.
4. SDs describe participant-to-participant variation; SEs describe uncertainty in an arm mean. They were not interchanged without the corresponding $\sqrt{n}$ conversion.
5. Correlations and covariances required for propagation were not reported. All propagation therefore used an assumption of independence, that is, covariance terms were set to zero. This is a practical transparent assumption and is not necessarily conservative.
6. First-order delta-method propagation was used for nonlinear transformations.

For a derived quantity $g(\mathbf{X})$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}\{g(\mathbf{X})\}
\approx
\nabla g(\boldsymbol{\mu})^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
\nabla g(\boldsymbol{\mu}).
$$

In the implemented calculations, off-diagonal elements of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ were set to zero unless structural dependence could be removed algebraically.

# Notation

| Symbol | Definition |
|---|---|
| $E$ | Daily energy intake, kcal/day |
| $p$ | Proportion of energy obtained from protein, from 0 to 1 |
| $D$ | Dietary protein intake, g/day |
| $S$ | Supplemental protein intake, g/day |
| $s$ | Fixed absolute supplemental dose, g/day |
| $d$ | Fixed relative supplemental dose, g/kg/day |
| $T$ | Total absolute protein intake, g/day |
| $W$ | Body mass, kg |
| $R$ | Total relative protein intake, g/kg/day |
| $B$ | Baseline protein intake |
| $\Delta$ | Reported change in protein intake |
| $F$ | Follow-up protein intake |
| $n$ | Relevant arm sample size |
| $k$ | Number of reported time points averaged |

# Converting supplement schedules to a daily dose

When a fixed amount $s_j$ was administered $f_j$ times per week, the mean daily dose was

$$
S_{\text{day}}=\frac{\sum_j f_js_j}{7}.
$$

This includes schedules that differed between training and non-training days. When a product contained several protein-bearing components, their protein contributions were summed before the weekly schedule was converted. Non-protein placebo components were not counted as protein. A fixed prescribed dose was treated as exact unless the study reported between-participant variation or adherence variability in the consumed dose.

# Combining or averaging reported values

## Arithmetic mean across time points

When the intervention exposure was represented by the arithmetic mean of $k$ reported intervention time points,

$$
\bar X=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^k X_j.
$$

Under the prespecified independence assumption, the uncertainty of that mean was

$$
s_{\bar X}=\frac{\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^k s_j^2}}{k},
$$

where every $s_j$ was on the same uncertainty scale (all SDs or all SEs). Thus, two values require division by 2, three by 3, four by 4, and five by 5 after summing variances.

## Combining groups

For groups with sizes $n_j$ and means $\bar X_j$, the combined mean was

$$
\bar X=\frac{\sum_j n_j\bar X_j}{\sum_j n_j}.
$$

When a common participant SD was required, the pooled within-group SD was

$$
s_p=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_j(n_j-1)s_j^2}{\sum_j n_j-J}},
$$

where $J$ is the number of groups. This does not add between-group mean differences and therefore represents the pooled within-group SD.

# Converting reported uncertainty

## SE and SD

$$
SD=SE\sqrt{n}, \qquad SE=\frac{SD}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

The relevant $n$ was the number contributing to the reported mean. An already reported SE was not divided by $\sqrt n$ a second time.

## Confidence interval to SE

For a two-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval $[L,U]$,

$$
SE=\frac{U-L}{2c},
$$

where $c=t_{1-\alpha/2,df}$ when an appropriate degrees of freedom was available and $c=1.96$ for the implemented large-sample 95% CI approximation. A corresponding participant SD was obtained only by $SD=SE\sqrt n$.

## Range to SD

When only a minimum $a$, maximum $b$, and sample size $n$ were available, the implemented estimator was

$$
SD\approx\frac{b-a}{2\Phi^{-1}\left(\frac{n-0.375}{n+0.25}\right)}.
$$

This was used only where the source quantity was treated as an observed range rather than a confidence interval.

# Deriving protein intake

## Energy intake and percentage energy from protein

Protein provides approximately 4 kcal/g, so

$$
D=\frac{Ep}{4}.
$$

If $p$ was fixed,

$$
s_D=\frac{p}{4}s_E.
$$

If both $E$ and $p$ varied, independence gave

$$
s_D=\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{p^2s_E^2+E^2s_p^2}.
$$

The product of reported means approximates the mean of the participant-level product because the unavailable covariance term was set to zero.

## Fixed absolute supplement

For a fixed supplement of $s$ g/day,

$$
T=D+s, \qquad s_T=s_D.
$$

If dietary protein was reported directly in g/kg/day but the supplement was fixed in g/day,

$$
R=R_{\text{diet}}+\frac{s}{W}.
$$

Under independence,

$$
s_R\approx\sqrt{s_{R_{\text{diet}}}^2+\left(\frac{s\,s_W}{W^2}\right)^2}.
$$

## Fixed relative supplement and structural dependence

For a supplement prescribed as a fixed $d$ g/kg/day,

$$
R=\frac{D+dW}{W}=\frac{D}{W}+d.
$$

The shared body mass must be cancelled before propagation. Under independence of dietary protein and body mass,

$$
s_R\approx\sqrt{\left(\frac{s_D}{W}\right)^2+\left(\frac{D\,s_W}{W^2}\right)^2}.
$$

Using $T=D+dW$ and then propagating $T/W$ as if $T$ and $W$ were independent is not equivalent: it omits their structural covariance and overstates the body-mass contribution.

## General absolute intake converted to g/kg/day

For an absolute total $T$ that was not itself constructed from the same body mass,

$$
R=\frac{T}{W},
$$

and under independence,

$$
s_R\approx\sqrt{\left(\frac{s_T}{W}\right)^2+\left(\frac{T\,s_W}{W^2}\right)^2}
=R\sqrt{\left(\frac{s_T}{T}\right)^2+\left(\frac{s_W}{W}\right)^2}.
$$

The ratio of arm means is a first-order approximation to the mean of participant-level ratios.

## Baseline plus change

When baseline and change were in the same units,

$$
F=B+\Delta, \qquad s_F=\sqrt{s_B^2+s_\Delta^2}.
$$

When baseline was in g/kg/day and change in g/day,

$$
F_{\text{rel}}=B_{\text{rel}}+\frac{\Delta_{\text{abs}}}{W},
$$

$$
s_{F,\text{rel}}\approx\sqrt{s_B^2+\left(\frac{s_\Delta}{W}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\Delta\,s_W}{W^2}\right)^2}.
$$

# Deriving body mass

When fat mass and fat-free mass were reported,

$$
W=FM+FFM, \qquad s_W=\sqrt{s_{FM}^2+s_{FFM}^2}.
$$

When fat-free mass $L$ and body-fat proportion $P$ were reported,

$$
W=\frac{L}{1-P},
$$

$$
s_W\approx\sqrt{\left(\frac{s_L}{1-P}\right)^2+\left(\frac{L\,s_P}{(1-P)^2}\right)^2}.
$$

These identities require a true fat-free-mass measure. Lean soft tissue without bone mineral content is not identical to total fat-free mass.

# Participant SDs and arm-mean SEs

Participant SDs were propagated from participant-level SD inputs. Arm-mean SEs were propagated from SE inputs. When only a derived participant SD was available, the arm-mean SE was $SD/\sqrt n$. Conversely, an SE recovered from a confidence interval was entered on the SE scale unless it was explicitly converted to an SD with $\sqrt n$.

The workbook contains both uncertainty types because the participant SD describes exposure heterogeneity within an arm, whereas the SE describes sampling uncertainty in the arm mean used as a meta-regression exposure. They answer different questions and should not be substituted for one another.

# Absolute-exposure variables used in the additional analyses

The preregistered primary analysis uses achieved total protein intake relative to body mass (g/kg/day). Two additional, explicitly exploratory exposure programmes were subsequently added: achieved total protein intake in g/day and prescribed supplemental protein in g/day. These variables were constructed from the combined, audited arm-characteristics data rather than by replacing or rewriting the relative-intake exposure used in the primary analysis.

## Achieved total protein intake in g/day

For each arm, a directly reported positive intervention total in g/day was preferred. When this was unavailable, total intake was reconstructed from the reported intervention intake relative to body mass and the arm mean body mass:

$$
T_{\mathrm{achieved}}=R_{\mathrm{intervention}}W.
$$

If an arm-mean SE was not reported directly, it was recovered from the corresponding participant SD and the baseline arm sample size. When total g/day was reconstructed and both component SEs were available, the implemented first-order independent-input approximation was

$$
SE(T_{\mathrm{achieved}})
\approx
\sqrt{\{W\,SE(R_{\mathrm{intervention}})\}^2+
      \{R_{\mathrm{intervention}}\,SE(W)\}^2}.
$$

The same hierarchy was applied to baseline intake: a reported baseline value in g/day was preferred and otherwise calculated as baseline g/kg/day multiplied by mean body mass. This baseline value supports the assignment-derived sensitivity exposure

$$
T_{\mathrm{assignment}}=T_{\mathrm{baseline}}+S_{\mathrm{prescribed}}.
$$

Thus, achieved total intake and assignment-derived total intake are deliberately different variables. The former uses the intervention-period dietary assessment and is post-randomisation; the latter combines baseline intake with the prescribed increment and is an intention-to-treat-like proxy. They are compared on a common set of reconstructable arms in the corresponding sensitivity analysis.

## Prescribed supplemental protein in g/day

The absolute-supplement exposure is the protein supplied by the assigned product or schedule, expressed as a calendar-day average. The schedule and composition calculations in the study register below therefore feed this exposure directly. The following source rules were applied:

1. a reported non-negative product protein dose was retained for protein, placebo, control, or other comparator arms;
2. a missing dose was set to zero only when the arm was explicitly classified as control or placebo;
3. reported protein in a comparator product was retained rather than overwritten with zero; and
4. a missing dose in a protein arm remained missing.

An otherwise eligible row contributed to the supplementation analysis only when its supplement-dose value was complete and its outcome-specific study included at least one arm classified as a protein intervention with a positive prescribed dose. This prevents all-zero studies with no randomised protein contrast from determining the supplementation dose-response. The exposure represents prescribed supplemental protein, not total achieved intake and not an adherence-adjusted consumed dose. Because the prescribed dose was treated as fixed, no errors-in-variables model was added for this exposure.

## Scaling used for modelling

The absolute scales were transformed only for numerical conditioning. Achieved total intake was centred at 78.785 g/day, the audited median among eligible unique control or placebo arms, and model coefficients were expressed per 50 g/day. Prescribed supplementation was centred at its natural zero and expressed per 25 g/day. These transformations change coefficient units but not the underlying fitted dose-response functions.

The original 26-member candidate registry was otherwise mapped to the absolute scales, except for the eight linear-spline candidates whose knot was fixed at 1.6 g/kg/day. That body-mass-relative threshold has no unique g/day equivalent, so it was not transferred to either absolute scale. Eighteen candidates per outcome were therefore retained for each applicable absolute-exposure family.

## Additional limitations of the absolute reconstruction

The reconstruction $T=RW$ assumes independence of the arm-mean estimates because their covariance was not reported. Where a published relative intake was itself calculated using the same body mass, $R$ and $W$ are structurally dependent; multiplying them and applying the independent-input formula may then double-count part of the body-mass uncertainty. The extraction files do not identify this provenance consistently enough to recover the covariance arm by arm. Directly reported g/day values were therefore preferred, the source of every selected value and SE was retained in the absolute-exposure audit, and analyses using reconstructed values are interpreted as sensitivity analyses rather than replacements for the preregistered relative-intake analysis.

# Study-level calculation register

## Method codes

| Code | Implemented calculation |
|---|---|
| D1 | supplement dose calculated from reported dose, frequency, protein composition, and/or body mass; weekly schedules were divided by 7 |
| P1 | weighted mean and/or pooled uncertainty |
| A1 | arithmetic mean across reported intervention time points |
| A2 | uncertainty of an arithmetic mean under independence |
| B1 | body mass or body-mass uncertainty derived from reported components |
| U2 | 95% confidence interval converted to an SE (and to an SD only when multiplied by sqrt(n)) |
| U3 | range converted to an SD with a sample-size-adjusted normal-quantile estimator |
| R1 | absolute intake converted to g/kg/day with ratio propagation |
| S1 | fixed absolute supplement added to dietary intake in g/day |
| S2 | fixed absolute supplement added to a directly reported relative dietary intake |
| S3 | fixed relative supplement added directly in g/kg/day |
| S3* | weight-based supplement; mean is correct but the workbook uncertainty formula requires the structural-dependence correction described below |
| E1 | grams of protein reconstructed from energy intake and protein energy percentage |
| C1 | follow-up intake reconstructed from baseline plus an absolute change |

# 2026 review update extraction

The trials added in the 2026 update were extracted into a separate workbook while the previously completed analyses remained frozen. The following calculations were checked against the update-study reports and are recorded in that workbook. The updated analyses combine the two workbooks in memory and use the same preparation pipeline for both.

## Study 165: Huijing et al. (2026)

The Impact of Oral Whey Protein and Yeast Protein Supplementation for 6 Months on Skeletal Muscle Mass, Strength, and Function in the Elderly: A Randomized, Controlled, Parallel Study. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/fsn3.71552.

Method codes: `R1`, `S1`.

The longitudinal dietary-intake table was used rather than reconstructing intake from the nominal product composition. At week 24, the whey-protein arm reported 63.4 (SD 2.2) g/day dietary protein and 15.2 (SD 0.3) g/day supplemental protein; the yeast-protein arm reported 55.9 (SD 18.7) and 15.8 (SD 0.4) g/day, respectively; and the control arm reported 54.4 (SD 9.2) g/day dietary protein with no supplement. Under independence,

$$
T=D+S, \qquad s_T=\sqrt{s_D^2+s_S^2}.
$$

The total was divided by the arm mean baseline body mass recorded in the participant-characteristics table, and uncertainty was propagated with `R1`. This gave:

| Arm | $T$, g/day | $s_T$, g/day | $R$, g/kg/day | $s_R$, g/kg/day | $SE_R$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Whey protein | 78.6 | 2.220 | 1.278 | 0.166 | 0.0298 |
| Yeast protein | 71.7 | 18.704 | 1.142 | 0.340 | 0.0620 |
| Control | 54.4 | 9.200 | 0.916 | 0.173 | 0.0311 |

The retained workbook formulas are:

- `W10`: `=63.4+E10`; `Y10`: `=SQRT(2.2^2+0.3^2)`; `Z10`: `=W10/L10`; `AB10`: `=SQRT((Y10/L10)^2+(W10*N10/L10^2)^2)`
- `W11`: `=55.9+E11`; `Y11`: `=SQRT(18.7^2+0.4^2)`; `Z11`: `=W11/L11`; `AB11`: `=SQRT((Y11/L11)^2+(W11*N11/L11^2)^2)`
- `W12`: `=54.4`; `Y12`: `=9.2`; `Z12`: `=W12/L12`; `AB12`: `=SQRT((Y12/L12)^2+(W12*N12/L12^2)^2)`

## Study 169: Patel et al. (2025)

A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled, Double-Blind Study of Phyllanthus Amarus in Combination with Whey Protein Isolate on Skeletal Muscle Strength in Active Males. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2147/OAJCT.S546033.

Method code: `D1`.

The 40 g product contained 92.5% protein, giving `E20 = 40 * 0.925 = 37` g/day. Total relative protein intake could not be reconstructed because body mass and total dietary protein intake were not reported; the study therefore remains unavailable to the relative-intake dose-response analysis unless those inputs become available.

## Study 170: Seyhan et al. (2026)

The combined effects of whey protein and collagen supplementation on bone mineral density and muscle mass in resistance-trained men: a randomized controlled trial. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1186/s13102-026-01846-y.

Method codes: `A1`, `A2`, `S2`.

Dietary intake was averaged across the two reported intervention measurements. Fixed supplemental protein was then added to the relative dietary intake. The supplement/body-mass component of uncertainty was retained:

$$
s_R=\sqrt{s_{R_{\mathrm{diet}}}^2+\left(\frac{s\,s_W}{W^2}\right)^2}.
$$

The resulting relative intakes (SDs) were 2.276 (0.0638), 2.140 (0.0744), 1.949 (0.0814), and 1.780 (0.0778) g/kg/day for the whey-plus-collagen, whey, collagen, and placebo arms, respectively. The extraction and formulas are retained for provenance, but this study is designated for exclusion from quantitative synthesis by author-group decision because of unresolved data-integrity concerns.

## Study 171: Svensson et al. (2026)

Effect of Intra-Workout Protein-Carbohydrate Co-Ingestion Versus Isocaloric Carbohydrate During Resistance Training on Muscle Fibre Hypertrophy and Oxidative Capacities in Young Men: A Randomized Controlled Trial. DOI: https://doi.org/10.3390/nu18142307.

Method codes: `D1`, `S2`.

The report gives protein consumed per completed workout and the mean number of sessions completed during the 56-day intervention. The workout-specific protein was therefore converted to a calendar-day average:

$$
S_{\mathrm{day,CHO:P}}=32.9\times\frac{24.8}{56}=14.57\ \mathrm{g/day},
$$

$$
S_{\mathrm{day,CHO}}=19.4\times\frac{26.3}{56}=9.111\ \mathrm{g/day}.
$$

These values include the protein supplied during and after each completed session. They were added to the intervention dietary values from Supplementary Table S1, giving 1.413 (SD 0.280) and 1.678 (SD 0.259) g/kg/day, respectively. The retained formulas are `E25 = 32.9*(24.8/56)`, `Z25 = 1.23+(E25/L25)`, `E26 = 19.4*(26.3/56)`, and `Z26 = 1.56+(E26/L26)`. The stored SDs also include the supplement/body-mass term from `S2`.

## Study 172: Vaithanomsat et al. (2025)

Enhancing Muscle Strength and Reducing Inflammation: The Combined Effects of Hydrolyzed House Cricket Protein Supplementation and Concurrent Training in Older Women. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/fsn3.70984.

Method codes: `D1`, `S1`, `S2`.

The 30 g supplement contained 76.96% protein, so the fixed protein dose was

$$
s=0.7696\times30=23.088\ \mathrm{g/day}.
$$

For the protein-only and protein-plus-concurrent-training arms, this was added to the reported intervention dietary intake. Relative intake was 1.630 and 1.509 g/kg/day, respectively. The final audit added the previously omitted body-mass component to the relative-intake SDs:

- `AB28`: `=SQRT(0.1^2+(E28*N28/L28^2)^2)` = 0.1192 g/kg/day;
- `AB30`: `=SQRT(0^2+(E30*N30/L30^2)^2)` = 0.0492 g/kg/day.

The zero in the second formula is the rounded dietary-intake SD reported for that arm; the uncertainty is nevertheless non-zero because the fixed absolute supplement is divided by a variable body mass.

# Audit interpretation and limitations

The register identifies the calculations that remain directly auditable from workbook formulas. Blank formula fields do not necessarily imply that a value was directly reported: some earlier extraction calculations were pasted as values. Such cases require source-level verification and should not be described as formula-reproducible.

All uncertainty formulas in this document use independence because correlations and covariances were unavailable. This includes repeated measurements averaged across time. The independence assumption is not itself treated as a data error, but its direction of bias depends on the transformation and the unobserved correlation.

The structural-dependence corrections for Studies 26 and 54 were verified.
